title: Zamzam, again
hook: pilgrims drink Zamzam, for whatever purpose it is drunk (Ibn Majah)

segments.voice: Yesterday: two rak'ahs behind Ibrahim's station, a stillness after the circling. Your line: where ibrahim stood.

A glass of water, and a question before you drink it: what is this for? On an ordinary day, the question never comes up. Thirst, habit, the meeting running long. But a hadith in the collection of Ibn Majah makes it matter. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have said that the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for. Not just thirst. Whatever the drinker brings to it. You met this well back on day forty. Today it comes back, in the middle of the pilgrimage, with a new job.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER.` → `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.`

segments.voice: First, where the water comes from. Zamzam is a well inside the sacred mosque in Mecca, close to the Ka'ba. In a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas tells how it first appeared: a mother alone in a dry valley with her baby, searching, and water breaking out of the ground. Her search is tomorrow's story. Second, the Prophet at the well. Jabir's account of the pilgrimage, in Sahih Muslim, has him coming to the people of his own clan as they drew water at Zamzam and gave it out. They handed him a bucket, and he drank. Ibn Abbas adds, in Bukhari, that he was the one who gave the Prophet Zamzam, and that the Prophet drank it standing. A man, a bucket, a crowd, a drink. Third, the hadith from Ibn Majah. Some pilgrims take it literally. They stand by the taps and fountains, and before they drink, or while they drink, they ask for something. Healing for someone at home. Knowledge. Forgiveness. A child. Some carry bottles of it home for the people who couldn't come. Scholars have discussed the grading of this hadith, and readers take it in different ways; the habit it has formed is easy to see at the fountains. Fourth, what changes. Nothing about the glass is different. The water is still water. What changes is that the drinker stops, names a purpose, and turns a reflex into a request.
screen: `A WELL NEAR THE KA'BA.` · `A BUCKET, AND HE DRANK.` · `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.` · `A REFLEX TURNED INTO A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Hold a glass of ordinary water, if you have one, and before you drink, name one thing you hope for, for yourself or for someone else, plainly and quietly. If you pray, make it a du'a in your own words and say bismillah; if not, just name the hope. Then drink slowly.
Zamzam. The well beside the Ka'ba, whose water, the hadith says, is for whatever it is drunk for. Today's word.
Your line: drink with intention. The water stays the same; the drinker changes. That's day eleven twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Pilgrims drink Zamzam water in the sacred mosque, often making a du'a before drinking, and some bring containers of it home to share with family and friends.

options: The water's the same; a hadith says it's for whatever it's drunk for.
Because pilgrims aren't allowed to drink anything else during Hajj.
Because Zamzam is only for healing; drinking it for thirst is wrong.

notes: Ibn Majah 3062 ('the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for'): confirm number; its grading is discussed by hadith scholars, and the script says so without naming a grade.
Bukhari 3364 (Ibn Abbas: Hajar, the baby and the water appearing): kept brief, since sa'y is tomorrow; confirm number.
Sahih Muslim 1218 (Jabir: the Prophet came to Banu Abd al-Muttalib drawing Zamzam, they gave him a bucket and he drank): confirm.
Bukhari 1637 (Ibn Abbas: 'I gave the Prophet Zamzam and he drank standing'): confirm number.
'Some carry bottles of it home' is general color; check or soften.
Earlier days on this path covered Zamzam (hence 'again'); the angle here is the Ibn Majah hadith and intention.
